# `unused-suppression`

<!-- rule-docs:header (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
Tier: style · Profile: idiomatic · Default: off · Fixes: quick fix · Options: none

Reports a suppression directive, or a rule it names, that suppressed no finding
of an enabled rule.
<!-- /rule-docs:header -->

## Why it matters

A suppression outlives the finding it was written for: the code is fixed or
moved, the rule stops firing there, and the directive keeps hiding whatever
the rule would report on that line in the future. A stale directive also tells
readers that something here is wrong when nothing is.

## When it fires

A directive is judged after every finding it could suppress is known. Each
rule a `disable`, `disable-line`, `disable-next-line` or `disable-file`
directive names is reported when the rule is enabled for the file but none of
its findings fell under the directive; the other names of the same directive
are judged on their own, and the quick fix removes the unused name, or the
whole directive when it names nothing else.

The file pass judges the rules only it reports, and the project check judges
the rules only whole-project analysis reports. A rule that is off for the
file, a rule that both passes report (the lifecycle rules refined with
cross-file summaries), the imported deprecations and module members the
project check adds, and `non-idiomatic-file-name` are never judged. A
directive that names no rule or `all` is judged only when none of those later
rules is enabled, which in practice means only in a pass that runs nothing
else. Directives naming `unused-suppression` itself are never reported, and a
directive cannot suppress its own report.

<!-- rule-docs:footer (generated by `zig build rule-docs`) -->
## Example

```zig
fn answer() u32 {
    // zig-analyzer: disable-next-line
    return 42;
}
```
